pages.text: Ebenezer could type faster than he could think. All day, his thumbs flew across the keys: short words, funny spellings, hundreds of messages. He felt like a champion at it. Then, on Monday, Mr Quarcoo handed back the mock English paper. Ebenezer’s informal letter had a big red circle at the top. “What is this?” he asked. “Read it,” said Mr Quarcoo, kindly.

“What is this?” he asked.
“Read it,” said Mr Quarcoo, kindly.
pages.alt: A boy holds a marked exam paper with a red circle at the top while a teacher stands beside him.

pages.text: Ebenezer read his own letter. It was full of short, chatty spellings and little pictures. He had written the word “you” as one letter. He had written “before” with a number. He had written “going to” as “gonna”. He had even ended with a row of laughing faces. His cheeks grew warm. “It sounded fine in my head,” he said. “It sounds fine in a chat,” said Mr Quarcoo. “It does not sound fine in an exam.”

pages.text: Mr Quarcoo pinned two headings on the board: Chat Voice and Exam Voice. “You already have both,” he said. “You speak differently to your friends than to your grandmother, and you dress differently for a party than for church. Language works the same way. Chat voice is for friends and phones. Exam voice is for markers, who cannot see your face or hear your tone. They only have your words.”

pages.text: Priscilla wrote a list on the board. Chat only: “u”, “ur”, “b4”, “pls”, “tnx”, “gonna”, “wanna”, “lol”, “omg”, and the pictures. Exam safe: “you”, “your”, “before”, “please”, “thank you”, “going to”, “want to”, and strong full words such as “amused” and “astonished”. “If you are not sure,” said Priscilla, “use the longer, fuller form. It is always safe.”

pages.text: Ebenezer raised his hand. “What about the way we speak at home, sir? The mixed language, the pidgin?” Mr Quarcoo smiled. “That is a real and rich way of speaking, and it belongs to you. But in an English exam, write standard English. Think of it as a different outfit for a different occasion.” Ebenezer grinned. “Code-switching,” he said. “Exactly,” said Mr Quarcoo.

pages.text: The class turned it into a game called Translate. One student read a chatty sentence, and the others had to rewrite it in exam voice. “See u b4 the party, lol” became “I will see you before the party, and I look forward to it.” By the end of the lesson, the whole class was laughing and, without noticing, had learned thirty new full words.

pages.text: That evening, Ebenezer rewrote his letter, starting with his address and the date. “No. 6, Hill Street, Ho. 2nd July, 2027. Dear Teiko, I hope you are well. I am writing to invite you to my birthday party on Saturday at four o’clock. We will play football, eat jollof rice and listen to music. I would be delighted if you could come. Please reply as soon as you can. Your friend, Ebenezer.” Mr Quarcoo read it and nodded. “Warm, clear and complete,” he said. “Full marks for voice.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: standard contractions such as “won’t” and “can’t” appear in some school letters, but full forms such as “will not” and “cannot” are the safest choice if you are unsure. Keep chat spelling, number-and-letter words, the at-sign, laughing faces and pidgin for your friends. Ebenezer still types fast, but now he has two voices. The end.
